utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Tecla Benjamin, Chester Stamp, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager, Kimberly Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. And could we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the appearances for the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to greet everyone in the courtroom, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence teams, and the accused. And naturally, all the administrative personnel, and in particular the interpreters, who are doing a good job. We have to carry on with our examination, but we will first render an oral decision about the question that was raised yesterday with regard to how to tender documents into evidence. So in the light of what was said yesterday, the Trial Chamber would like to point out that both the Defence and the Prosecution submitted a motion concerning the manner of proceeding when tendering documents into evidence. In order to save time in the course of the proceedings, and in particular when thousands of documents are presented, the parties requested that the Trial Chamber state its position with regard to this matter. The Trial Chamber took into consideration the relevant elements, the relevant provisions in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, in particular Rule 90(F), which provides that the Trial Chamber can control the manner of examining a witness and the manner of presenting evidence, as well as the order of interrogating witnesses to make the examination, the presentation of evidence effective for the determination of truth and to avoid needless consumption of time. And for the foregoing reasons, the Trial Chamber renders the following decision, which is to be respected by both parties: The consolidated list drawn up by the Prosecution, the list of all the documents, the documents that were provided to General Reinhardt, the expert witness, as well as all the other documents or exhibits must be provided to the Trial Chamber on the 10th of March -- by the 10th of March, 2004, at the latest. The Prosecution must mention in this consolidated list the exhibits that have already been admitted into evidence or that are in the process of being identified. A definitive number or temporary number may already have been given to these documents by the registrar. The Defence must state its position with regard to this list before the 25th of March, 2004, at the latest, and they must indicate in particular which documents or exhibits are not being contested by the Defence and they must indicate which documents or exhibits are contested by the Defence. The Defence will have 15 days after this consolidated list has been presented. In the course of the hearing that will be held on Thursday, the 8th of April, 2004, the Trial Chamber will rule on the matter of tendering these documents into evidence and will request that the registrar on that date - on the 8th of April, 2004 - give an exhibit number for the documents that aren't contested by the Defence and the registrar will be asked to mark the documents that are contested for identification. The procedure just described shall only concern the exhibits that the Prosecution is preparing to present when calling witnesses after the week that starts on the 19th of April, 2004. The Prosecution will continue up until the 8th of April, 2004, to tender its documents into evidence in accordance with the procedure that is currently being followed when the Prosecution calls its witnesses. The Trial Chamber would also like to state that it desires to have a list of documents that the Prosecution intends to present when a witness is testifying before this witness actually testifies. To this effect, the internal memorandum from the Prosecution, which concerns, and I quote, "the order in which witnesses will be appearing" should be completed and mention should be made of the exhibits that they intend to use when examining each witness in the course of the week, from Monday to Friday. Just to give you an example: In the memorandum that I'm showing the parties you can see that a number of witnesses have been scheduled for next week. The names of the witnesses are mentioned. In brackets next to the name one should indicate the documents that the Prosecution intends to present. This document, drafted in this manner, won't be binding on the Prosecution in that the Prosecution can present exhibits at the eleventh hour, since circumstances might be such. So the fact that reference is made to a number of documents next to a name doesn't mean that the Prosecution cannot add other documents if it so desires. The oral decision that the Trial Chamber has just rendered shall not concern the exhibits presented by a party in the course of its cross-examination. In order to avoid wasting any time when the cross-examination is being conducted, the Trial Chamber would like to remind the Defence that when cross-examining, when the Defence presents an exhibit, they must state the origin of the document - that is to say, the source, the date, et cetera - they must mention any other useful information concerning the document. And in addition, they must inform the Trial Chamber of the relevance of the document and must provide grounds for the document's relevance. So I'd like to ask everyone to reread the transcript very carefully, because it might appear a little complicated. But the Trial Chamber has taken note of the comments made by both parties, and it is the Trial Chamber's opinion that this procedure could have a beneficial effect, as far as tendering documents into evidence is concerned, and it would enable us to save time. I think that you have understood me correctly. Up until the 19th of April, we will proceed as we have done to date. And as of the 19th of April, we shall start applying this new procedure. We can now call the witness into the courtroom. Could the usher lower the blinds, to prevent the witness from being seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down. We are in open session, but protective measures are in place. If Mr. Stamp thinks it is necessary that we should go into private session, you should ask us to do so, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last time you were here, Witness, you were telling us about a beating inflicted upon you about five days after you arrived at the furniture salon. Who, or which group, beat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw two guards who were there during the day and another two persons. I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were the other two persons in uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say what type of uniform they had on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Ordinary camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there anything that indicated to which unit they belonged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't even see, because it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that many other prisoners were beaten, sometimes five to six per night. Do you remember any of them beaten in any particularly severe way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that that night five or six persons were taken out. Mladen Havranek was the last one, and he died after having been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, tell us about that night. You said you remember that night five or six persons were taken out. Just tell us what happened that night, the night that Mladen Havranek died.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, he was the last person to be taken out. He was either the fifth or the sixth person. I can't remember exactly. But when someone went out, you could hear that person groaning. You could hear the person being beaten. And this was especially the case when Mladen was taken out. When they had finished beating the late Mladen, they sent him back down the stairs to the basement. But he wasn't able to reach the basement. He said something; I can't remember what. The other detainees who were in the basement approached him. He wasn't able to walk. He sat down. They thought that he wasn't well. They called a guard, told him he was dying. After that, they took him away somewhere, but I don't know what happened to him. I never saw him again, but I heard that he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who took him away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I suppose the persons who beat him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said you remained at the furniture salon for approximately 20 days, I think. Where were you taken, if anywhere, after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took me to the stadium, to the local stadium in Bugojno, under the stands, where they had the dressing rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was that stadium known by any particular name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bugojno Stadium, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it used by any particular team or sporting organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the Iskra Bugojno football team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you were taken there and put in the rooms underneath the stands, about how many persons were detained in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think I was one of the first. I was in the first group. At the time, they had already started arriving from other prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long did you remain as a detainee at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained there until the exchange on the 19th of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you remember approximately what date you arrived at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember the date. I've forgotten the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Approximately what month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in October, at the beginning of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in the period of time that you were detained there, approximately how many prisoners were there? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number was not always the same. There may have been between 300 and 400 people; it depended on the moment when you counted. Some were taken for forced labour. At the end, 350 people altogether left the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, while you were at the stadium, did you learn who was in charge of the facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gasal was one of the men in charge. I don't know his first name. I've forgotten. And Kukavica was the head of guards or something like that. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was Kukavica -- is Kukavica a first name or a surname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, do you know which unit manned -- withdrawn. The persons in charge, Gasal and Kukavica, were in charge of which unit? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. There were camp commanders or prison wardens. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, while you were there, how were the prisoners generally treated by these guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The treatment was different. Some guards were good; some were bad. At the very beginning, they would beat us more often. We would be taken out for beating more often.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Tell us how that was organised. Firstly, having been there for a few months, did you observe any pattern in who would be taken out, or did it appear to you to be at random?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know how they did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, how would they conduct the beatings? And by that I mean how was it organised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would call our names in the evening. That's what was happening at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when they called your names, what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would take people out and beat them in the corridor, outside the room where the detainees were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were any of the prisoners taken away from the stadium to any other location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were taken for interrogation. Some would return. Some went missing and their lot is not known, to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where were they taken to for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know - and I heard it from other detainees - they were taken to the BH Bank building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you know some of the persons who were taken there who did not return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know almost all of them, because they were with me there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stamp, when you ask a question about a person, maybe we should go into private session, because if he gives certain names that may identify your witness, you have the right to ask to go into private session, if you're going to be asking for names of certain people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think, though, that he'll be referring to persons who were members of the HVO units in Bugojno. That did not give away his identity at all. But perhaps I could ask him. That's the best way to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of some of those who were taken away and have not been seen since?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember the units that they were members of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were members -- actually, commanders of the military police, the 1st Battalion, the 2nd Battalion, intellectuals, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll take your advice, Mr. President, and ask that we go into closed session very briefly -- private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, were you and other detainees taken away from the stadium for any particular purpose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. People were taken to work, to dig trenches on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You were speaking generally now about people. Let's start with your own personal experience. Were you at any time taken anywhere in this regard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken twice or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The first time, where were you taken? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time, I was taken to Podripci. I believe that is the name of the village only front line towards Donji Vakuf, facing the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you volunteer to go, or were you taken against your will?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Against my will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, what -- how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten to fifteen days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what did you do while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were digging trenches and dugouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where were these trenches and dugouts in relation to the front line which you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned that you were taken to Podripci, a village in the vicinity of the front lines, to dig trenches. What I want to know is how far were these trenches and dugouts that you excavated from these front lines.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the very front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you went there, were you accompanied by guards from the stadium, or were you put in the custody of other persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were handed over to other persons, into their custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who were these other persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were predominantly men from the unit that was on that front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the unit of which army was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Maybe you didn't understand the question I'm asking. The front line that you worked on was occupied by which unit -- by which army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also mentioned that other persons were taken to other places. How did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having returned to the detention unit, I heard from other people that they had been taken to other places. We all knew each other, so we talked amongst ourselves and informed each other as to where people were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you told the places, the names of the places where these other persons were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken to Gornji Vakuf, some 50 of them, I believe. Some were also taken towards Kupres. I don't know the name of the line there, where they were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were you told what they were taken there to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, were you told if all of them returned alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, two people were killed and several were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The second time you were taken from the stadium, where were you taken to? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken to Pajic Polje, and we dug trenches in Duratbegovic Dolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And how far were these trenches that you dug from the front lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was also on the front line, just above Duratbegovic Dolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were engaged in this process, were you and any of the other prisoners exposed to any additional risk? That is, risk or danger in addition to digging trenches on the front line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three detainees were killed there and later on, when this was found out, we were all taken to the trenches to stand up straight so as to be well visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "so as to be well visible"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the top of that hill on that line, there were also some trenches, like dugouts --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there is a very significant error in translation, page 14, line 8. He said that "three detainees were killed there." I heard the witness saying that from that place three detainees had escaped and then they were punished -- the rest of them were punished by standing up. Since the witness is still here, I've heard his answer, can we have the witness repeat that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. It's not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said three detainees had escaped; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you were -- okay. You were explaining to us what you meant when you said that you were put to stand up straight so as to be well visible. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every trench or in every dugout two people were made to climb up on every dugout and we were made to stand there for an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you could be visible to whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the other side, the other side of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you say when you were eventually exchanged? Or just let me ask the question: When were you eventually exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 19 March 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have nothing further to ask you for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Defence for the cross-examination of this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have told us that you were made to stand up straight in the trenches. Who made that decision? The people who guarded you, their commander, or maybe you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in Pajic Polje at the time. Pajic Polje was a base, or maybe it was a forward command post. I don't know exactly what it was. That is some 2 kilometres away from the front line. From there, every day we would go to dig trenches in Dolac, and somebody must have issued that order from that school. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were in the stadium, you said that there were some 200 or 300 of you there. How many guards were there who guarded you at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They worked in shifts, and there was a different group every day. There may have been between five and ten of them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were between five and ten, and their task was to guard a number of prisoners; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But we were locked up, and we were behind bars. We couldn't escape. And there was also a fence erected in front of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the group in which you knew a number of people, nobody ever planned to escape.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not possible to escape from there. It would have been very difficult. We were behind bars. There was an iron gate which was locked. We were locked up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Defence, you have the floor again. Please make sure not to ask questions that might identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. ZC. My name is Edina Residovic, and I represent General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go into private session, please, as the first few questions might reveal the witness's identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. ZC, is it correct to say that the headquarters of the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade were located in Tito's villa, on the hill called Gorica above the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Battalion was located in the Vojin Paleksic Primary School?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The military police was in the Kalin Hotel in the centre of town; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO also had checkpoints in the villages in Cucici [phoen], Lova [phoen], Vrbanja, Bristovi and the surrounding areas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, together with the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In February 1993, in addition to your brigade, Home Guard units were formed in Bugojno; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, there were many factors that had an influence and resulted in an increase in tension between the army and the HVO; that is to say, between the Croatian and Bosniak population in the town. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Many refugees arrived in the town and in the immediate vicinity of Bugojno, in Gornji Vakuf. There was permanent fighting between the army and the HVO. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the military police, you were a member of mixed commissions together with the police from the BH army and you tried to calm the situation down --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to object, for the record, to this line of questioning. For the record, this witness has testified in this case about the condition of prison facilities in Bugojno. The questions tend to elicit evidence which is not relevant to the matters in issue in this particular trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if my learned colleague has a look at the transcript, he will realise that he also asked the witness whether he was a member of the military police and the witness also said that he worked with the army in order to solve certain difficulties, deal with certain incidents. I don't think that my question wasn't within the scope of the examination-in-chief, but I would like to hear your suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the transcript, at one point you asked him a question and you told him that as an HVO policeman he would go on patrol. And in line 3, page 19, he spontaneously said, "Yes, but I did that with the BH army." So the witness himself said that. The Defence's question was whether he was a member of a mixed commission. I think that this question can be put to him. That's really not a problem. We know that he was an HVO policeman, that he went on patrol with the army, and the Defence's question was whether he could confirm that he was a member of a commission. So please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. ZC, would it be correct to say that as a military policeman you went with members of the BH army military police to deal with incidents that occurred in Bugojno, and you participated with them in these joint commissions? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, we went on patrol and manned checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. ZC, are you aware of the fact that on the 17th of July, 1993, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the conflict that broke out at the checkpoint in Vrbanja spread beyond that area and engulfed the entire town of Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly the first time this occurred. Perhaps the first incident occurred earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These conflicts last from the 18th to the 27th of July, when the HVO headquarters finally surrendered, the HVO headquarters located in Tito's villa in Gorica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 27th or 28th, they withdrew then. I think it was the 28th of July. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of the conflict, you reported to the Croatian home, which wasn't far from the headquarters of the military police, in the Hotel Kalin. You reported there for your duties.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your group soon surrendered, around the 19th or 20th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's answer wasn't audible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The members of the army who captured you first took you to the basement in your home. That's where your base was located. And then they took you to the grammar school. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a building which was adjacent to it, perhaps about 15 metres from the Croatian home.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. ZC, I'm going to go back to a question that I have already asked you, because the interpreters have pointed out that they didn't hear your answer. The question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, try and speak up. When you answer, try to raise your voice a little so that the interpreters can hear you, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether it was correct to say that your group surrendered on the 19th or, rather, on the 20th of July. Your answer hasn't been recorded in the transcript, so could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was captured on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 19th. Yes. Witness, you have to be precise nevertheless, because there are two solutions: You were taken prisoner, or you surrendered. You could have surrendered and being a prisoner afterwards, or you were taken prisoner. What is the correct answer? It seems the Defence is saying that you surrendered, and it seems that you are saying that no, you were taken prisoner. So what are you actually telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know what you mean when you say "in the course of the fighting." I was captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that you were asked to surrender. You said there was fighting. You had a weapon. You had to surrender your weapons and raise your hands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Things are a little clearer now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by my colleague, you said that you were transferred from the grammar school to the furniture salon, and you told us what happened there. Would it be correct to say that the prisoners in the furniture salon were maltreated at night and that was the case for you as well? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the whole, you were not able to see or recognise the persons who would take the prisoners out and beat them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really recognise them, but sometimes they used lighters to shed a bit of light.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you could see that they were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. ZC, to say that before these conflicts members of the army in Bugojno often wore camouflage uniforms as well as policemen and HVO members but other people who were able to obtain such uniforms also wore them? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that you were visited in the furniture salon by some nuns? They brought you some food and some clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would come occasionally, but not frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. ZC, would it be correct to say that in fact you didn't know who had ordered the detainees to be placed in the grammar school or, rather, in the furniture salon, nor did you know who the guards' superiors were? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the BH army. Who else would it be? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't know who the individual persons were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back into private session, again, since the witness mentioned the names of some persons in private session. So I think that it would be appropriate for the Defence to put questions to the witness in private session too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. ZC, while you were at the stadium, were you visited by nuns, by Dr. Jadranka, and were families able to take food there for the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They'd bring us food, but it was difficult to get it through. Sometimes they would allow them to provide us with food.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. ZC, would it be correct to say that before you left for Podripci you reported to go and perform certain duties outside of the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to get out of the darkness and get a bit of air and see a little light.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you went to the village of Vrbanja, where you buried inhabitants from the village of Vrbanja who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that we dug tombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were then maltreated by the Muslim civilian population from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you returned, after having carried out this work, you spoke about it to a prisoner, who said that the civilians had also severely beaten Mario Zrno and they said that Mario Zrno died as a result of the injuries.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that, but that happened before I went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also don't know who decided that the Iskra Stadium should be used as a prison.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And similarly, you don't know who decided that the people guarding you should provide security for that prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Likewise, you don't know who the superiors of Gasal or, rather, Kukavica were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. ZC.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the other Defence team have any questions? Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't have any questions. As we anticipated, this witness hasn't testified about any charges with which Mr. Kubura is proceeded against in the indictment, so we have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. Mr. Stamp, is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No re-examination. May it please you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] Witness, this concludes your examination. You have answered the questions put to you by the Defence, by the Prosecution, and by the Chamber. Thank you for having come to The Hague as a witness for the Prosecution. We wish you a good trip home. Before you leave this courtroom, I'm going to ask the usher to lower the blinds. Witness, you can now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's almost time to have the break, so it would be best to have the break immediately. We will resume at five past 4.00, and we'll have a new witness who will be testifying at five past 4.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that for the next witness we don't have any particular protective measures, Mr. Withopf. Can you confirm that? The Chamber would like to greet Mrs. Benjamin, who has just joined us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It's correct, Mr. President. The Prosecution will not apply for protective measures in respect to the next witness. There are, however, a number of issues related to this witness my colleague, Mrs. Benjamin, would like to address.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this witness is, to put it simply, illiterate and a little bit fragile with respect to her appearance here. I have discussed with my colleagues on the other side with respect to the reading of the oath, how we are going to deal with it, and they have no objections to the oath being read to her. But I wish to ask the Chamber, at the Chamber's discretion, if the Court would allow me on certain occasions perhaps to lead the witness in certain areas, because -- because of her situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in open session. The Chamber would like to say that an order should be prepared for the transcript to be redacted. Mr. Registrar, please prepare such an order for me to sign. And I am going to ask the usher to place the partitions in order to shield the witness from the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going into private session because there is a procedure to follow. Private session, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Benjamin, you may now proceed. But since protective measures are in place, if any of your questions are such that they might reveal the witness's identity you should request that we go into private session in such cases. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Much obliged, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness ZD, could you tell the Judges if there came a time when village guards were formed in the village of Cukle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were village guards. Everyone protected his own house. There was a lack of trust among the people. No one trusted anyone anymore. So some of them protect their houses; others their own houses, although there were no disputes. That's what happened. Well, they sort of guarded their houses and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And to whom were these guards made against? Who were you guarding your homes against?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people were afraid. They were afraid of the Mujahedin, foreign troops. Since we had a neighbour who was some way away from our village, they had their headquarters in Mehurici and he started to bring them to his house down there. Our people found out about it, and then my husband went to his neighbour's, his Muslim neighbour's, and he said, "What's going on? Why should we be afraid of each other?" And then panic started spreading among the villagers. No one trusted anyone any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did there come a time when the guards separated, when the Croats went in their own direction and the Muslims went in their own direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did separate. They were together for a while, as they were afraid of the Serbs who were attacking everyone. And then as the Mujahedin were in Mehurici, they'd cry out to the men in our defence, the Territorial Defence, et cetera - I don't know what they were called - they'd cry out and say they were going to Mehurici together there. Our people didn't want to accept this. The Mujahedin were living there. It was a foreign army, foreign troops. They had come from these Arab countries, and that's how the people started separating from each other. No one trusted anyone any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we may need to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session now. I would like to point out something with regard to witnesses who have already testified. When questions are asked, we have found out on a number of occasions that witnesses have already testified before international courts or at The Hague but we haven't been informed of this by the Prosecution. And on two occasions this caused procedural problems. It would be desirable when the Prosecution meets the witnesses in the pre-trial stage they should check to see whether the witness has already been in The Hague or testified in a national court. Why? Because if a witness was heard in 1998 and then appears subsequently in the year 2000 or 2001, in the written statement naturally this won't be indicated. And if the Trial Chamber doesn't ask the witness about this or the witness doesn't mention it, then we won't know about it. So when the witness is met, one has to assess the situation, the legal situation, in order to be aware of all the relevant facts. Because if the witness has already been examined and has made a solemn declaration and has benefitted -- and has had protective measures, the Trial Chamber needs to be aware of the fact. So I know your task is complicated, because very often you see the witnesses at the very last minute, but you have to ask the witnesses about the situation because these are things that happened a long time ago. The investigations were conducted a long time ago. Many things may have happened. There may be a lot of new factors that appear. For example, that was the case when I asked the witness a minute ago where the witness was living. This was quite new information. So you must be aware of this information. You must find out about it when you see the witnesses. So you have to say when a witness appeared, "Witness X is appearing. This witness testified or hasn't already testified." This is in order to save time and to avoid discovering problems in the course of the proceedings. And naturally, when it is the Defence's turn, when the Defence will be calling witnesses, they will proceed in the same manner, to avoid such problems so that we don't realise that witnesses are called who have already testified in other proceedings. So I think that these elementary things that could enable us to save time and avoid problems. When problems arise, we will deal with them, naturally. But it would be best if we could anticipate problems. And this could involve asking witnesses questions about what had happened since you last spoke to them. You should ask the witness if there is any new information, et cetera. So this is what the Trial Chamber desires, and this would enable us to deal with these witnesses more efficiently in the future. As we have noted on several occasions, for some it's the first time they've been abroad and they have testified. Sometimes they are under stress. And this can be dealt with if we place the witness in a certain context, for example, if the witness has already testified. I think you're fully aware of this problem that in future we will no longer have to deal with these matters. There is perhaps a solution that we could find, but this is up to the parties. You could have a list of the witnesses who have testified in similar proceedings, for example, the one that we mentioned. And this would enable you to verify that your witness is not included in that list, and the Defence could proceed in the same manner. They could also check by consulting lists, and this would enable them to have access to the examination and to prepare their cross-examination. As you know, the Trial Chamber can't carry out this task because the proceedings involve the parties. The Trial Chamber doesn't guide the proceedings, as you are well aware. Such is the procedure. Otherwise, we would have dealt with this matter. We have another 25 minutes. Is there anything you would like to say? Mr. Bourgon, you wanted to talk to us about Rule 75 and inform the Trial Chamber about certain issues that have to do with protective measures. I don't know whether you would like to address this issue at the moment or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before I speak about Rule 75 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, I would like to say something about protective measures. Yesterday, when protective measures were requested for one witness, we informed the Trial Chamber that for the future cases we have to listen to somebody from the Victims and Witnesses Unit in order to receive some specific information about Bugojno, for example. Also, we've mentioned on several occasions that there is a need for either the Prosecution or Defence to provide objective information in order for us to be able to prepare in advance when it comes to the application for protective measures. In that sense, Mr. President, we have been informed earlier today by the Prosecution about the witnesses which are due to arrive within the course of the next two weeks, from the 1st to the 12th of March. On that list, some of the witnesses have already informed the Prosecution that they intend to apply for protective measures. We believe, Mr. President, that by all means the Prosecution has to inform us in advance about the reasons which underlie the request for protective measures, if possible in writing but not necessarily so. But in any case, we have to be informed in advance about the reasons for which protective measures are requested. This will enable us to prepare ourselves and see whether we are going to object to the request or not. And if a case may be, we will be able to prepare ourselves having at our disposal all the objective information. And we keep on saying that the objective information is necessary. Also, we can listen to the witness explain his reasons for requesting protective measures. In order to corroborate my words, I would also like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to some facts. The witness that we have heard today and that has been granted protective measures - and one of the reasons put forward by the Prosecution was that the witness was going to mention a number of the names of important persons from the region - the only person that the witness mentioned was the name of one person which is well known in the region, but in addition to that name nobody else was mentioned. So what we are asking for is at the moment we receive information and -- to the Chamber, for the Chamber to reach their decision, this information has to be verified in advance. It has to be checked in order to enable the Chamber to pass a clear decision with regard to the protective measures. And at the end, Mr. President, as far as the testimony under protective measures is concerned, my colleagues from Mr. Kubura's Defence team have mentioned on several occasions that it sometimes happens that witnesses are granted protective measures but, despite the protective measures that have been granted - or because of the protective measures, most of the testimonies take place behind a closed door. Today again the testimony that we've heard today has been because -- in closed session. We have to mention that - and you've already said that, Mr. President - The sides have to do their utmost in order to work in closed session only when it is necessary. In that way, we will avoid or we wish to avoid interruptions during a witness's testimony and keep on saying that maybe we could work in open session. The public nature of the -- of these trials is very important, as far as the Defence is concerned. I'm going to end with Rule 75, Mr. President. We don't know whether your interpretation of this Rule 75 is, as a matter of fact, your decision. At the same time, we have been informed by our colleagues who work on other cases - I don't have the information at my disposal today - however, we've heard from our colleagues that some other Chambers interpreted Rule 75 differently. The fact is that when it comes to the continuity of the application of protective measures, these measures are applied to the information provided by the witness rather than to the person of the witness. I cannot go into any further details; however, I can tell you that we have on several occasions requested access to information in some other cases - for example, the Blaskic, the Kordic, and the Kupreskic case - and we have applied Rule 75. This Rule has been altered on several occasions in order to facilitate applications for such requests. This has led to some very complicated discussions in order to allow the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic to access information in the Blaskic case - and the two cases overlap in several segments. Rule 75 starts from one case to another, and the Rule speaks about the request to access the following information in the following way: When one team wants to access information in another case, and when this is granted, then protective measures are still in place. Likewise, when in our case, for example, the Prosecution informs us pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii) and when they disclose evidence to us and when they disclose evidence from some other case in which the witness testified under protective measures, the Prosecution may tell us, "We are giving you this information because it is our obligation; however, bear in mind that this witness or these witnesses testified under protective measures." So information still remains confidential. In the Ljubicic case, which is the case that is -- that is still not in trial but in its pre-trial stage, we have been given access to information in this case. In that particular case, the Chamber has made a ruling in order to be sure that protective measures will apply to a request from the Defence team in this case - that is, the Kubura and Hadzihasanovic Defence teams - to sign and hand over to the Trial Chamber a report on the names of the Defence team so as to bind all the persons in those two Defence teams by the continuity of protective measures. I'm not saying that your interpretation of this Rule is erroneous. I'm just wondering whether your interpretation today is a decision or maybe at some point in time we may still present arguments once we check the situation in other cases, the cases that our colleagues have informed us about. They have told us that some witnesses that have been granted protective measures in the past may be granted protective measures at a later stage and vice versa. Mr. President, what I'm saying is that this is more of a question, a question that concerns Rule 75. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your submission, you have presented us with a number of issues, and the last concerns the application of Rule 75 over the course of time. If we read paragraphs (F) and (G) of Rule 75, this doesn't leave any doubts why. When protective measures are once granted, this is for the reasons that have to do with the safety of a witness or a victim and the fact that a witness may be afraid if -- for his safety if his testimony becomes public or for some other reasons. If this situation is taken into account by one Chamber, this happens at a time T-zero, for example in 1998, for this particular witness that we have just heard. And if we read Rule 75 very closely, this protection is valid at a certain period of time. And Rule 75 regulates that issue. If in the meantime there's some new elements, some new information, this -- the granted measures may be rescinded, may be augmented, or may be altered because the danger has increased or decreased. We have to go one step further. So the situation may be completely different in the meantime. What -- who is in charge of making this decision? Certainly not the second Trial Chamber, but the Trial Chamber which sits in the first case. And that is the situation. This Trial Chamber will certainly take into account what you have just told us, and we will look into the possibility of rendering a different decision bearing in mind the position that you have presented. In addition to that, in this particular case, witnesses may also say whether they wish for the protective measures to continue. We have seen that in one or two cases, as the situation may be different in a different case. For example, in a different case we still have to have the witness's approval, and this has to be clear. These are all very important issues. They have to be looked at very carefully. We have to see -- look at the jurisprudence from other cases. The Prosecution also has to inform us about their position with regard to this issue. The issue at hand is the interpretation of Rule 75. However, in this stage, when we are considering the objections that you have presented, we have -- mustn't forget that there's a hypothetical situation in which protective measures have been granted for a reason. For whatever reason, that the measures may be altered. However, the fear that was expressed when the protective measures were asked in the first place is confirmed. We are going to look at this very carefully, and we will hand down our decision on this issue. You have also mentioned another thing; however, the Chamber has already provided you with an answer on several occasions. The issue is that you want the Prosecution to provide you with a list of the persons for whom they will apply for protective measures. The Prosecution has answered that sometimes they only meet the witness on the day of their testimony or a day in advance, and in that case they really do not have the time to inform you about the protective measures that they will be applying for. It would be ideal for them to provide you with a written request with all the information in written form, and based on that written information we could make our decision. We have to bear in mind that some witnesses live very far, contact with them is made at the last moment. Then we have to resort to the oral procedure. We have tried to improve the situation by asking the witness to explain his situation when the witness arrives. On several occasions, you have also raised the issue of the local context, and your suggestion is that somebody from the Victims and Witness Unit should be heard here as a witness. This could be done from the procedural point of view speaking if the Prosecution tells us that they will ask for protective measures to be granted for a certain witness, here are the reasons; but the reasons will be corroborated by a certain staff member of this particular unit to come and testify before this Trial Chamber. This is how this procedure can be started. The Prosecution can ask a staff member of this unit to testify. They have to turn to their supervisor to allow them to do that. However, it is necessary for the person who is sent to testify to be competent and to be familiar with the situation, because if that person only tells us what they heard or what they read in the press, this is not enough. The Prosecution, I'm sure, will think about this question, which is very important. Mr. Withopf, do you have anything to say at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I just briefly address the issues have both been dealt with by both my learned colleague and by the Presiding Judge. In respect to Rule 75(F) and (G), the Prosecution shares the view of the Trial Chamber, as expressed some days ago, and the Prosecution strives to always inform the Trial Chamber in due course whether witnesses have testified earlier on and whether protective measures have been granted. Unfortunately, in the today's case, we had this unfortunate situation that the witness herself was not in a position to inform us, although asked, that protective measures were granted in the other case. As you know, Your Honours, the Prosecution always informs Defence counsel, at least at the stage when the Prosecution files confidentially its witness schedule, about the names of the witnesses who intend to ask the Prosecution to apply for protective measures. The reasons of such -- The reasons of the witnesses vary and they vary substantially. Some of the reasons we can only figure out and we can only elaborate on once the witness arrives here in The Hague and once the lawyers of the trial team were in a position to talk to the witness. And as Your Honours, and as Your Honour Mr. President already pointed out, we are in a situation that quite often we meet the witnesses only the day prior to the testimony. In respect to the request of the Defence to ask somebody from the Witness and Victims Section to provide information on the situation in certain areas, for example, in Bugojno, I don't think that the members of the Victims and Witness Section actually do have the knowledge to provide such information. The issues the Victims and Witness Section are dealing with are a bit different from assessing the threats our witnesses -- or the Prosecution witnesses may be exposed to in certain areas. Again, the Prosecution is continuing to, at the earliest opportunity, to inform both the Defence counsel and the Trial Chamber about the names of protective witnesses -- or of witnesses who wish to have protective measures. In respect to the witnesses for tomorrow - and for that purpose, may I please ask to go into private session, since I want to provide some additional information?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of February, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.57 p.m.
